tooltips.Success metric: Something measurable before and after: a number, percentage, time, or frequency.
tooltips.AS-IS: As it happens now, in practice, on a normal day.
tooltips.Ideal, not actual: Mapping how the process should work instead of how it works.
tooltips.Trigger: What starts the process: a message, a form, a date.
tooltips.Steps: The path from trigger to result; three to seven are usually enough.
tooltips.Output: What comes out at the end, and to whom.
tooltips.Field template: A fixed set of fields; fits when you know the process and need a fast decision.
tooltips.BPMN: A standard for process diagrams, shared across tools and teams.
tooltips.Eight fields: Same spirit as the five-field template from Lesson 1, now for a whole process.
tooltips.Owner: Keeps a policy or document current.
tooltips.Sensitivity: One of four levels: PUBLIC, INTERNAL, CONFIDENTIAL, RESTRICTED. It decides what may go to an AI tool.
tooltips.Existing controls: Checks in place today; "no formal control" is valid.
tooltips.Gaps: What is missing or unclear; "unclear" is allowed.
tooltips.Field 8: Guardrail: answer accuracy stays at or above 95% in a QA sample.
tooltips.Baseline: The current state, even if estimated.
tooltips.Handoff: The moment responsibility passes from one role to another.
tooltips.Bottleneck: A step limited by the slowest resource.
tooltips.good-fit kind: Unstructured to structured · Low-risk decision points · Handoffs with delay or loss.

segments.narration: A team has a slow, painful process. A faster technology arrives, and they put it on top of the process as it is. The problem doesn't go away. It gets locked in, faster and at a larger scale.
segments.build: Messy chain; bolt 'faster tech' lands: 'same mess, faster'

segments.narration: In 1990, Harvard Business Review published an article called Reengineering Work: Don't Automate, Obliterate. Obliterate means wipe out. The principle: if you run new technology on a broken process without taking it apart first, you only speed up the inefficiency you already have. It was written about ordinary computing. It applies to AI just as well.

Case one. The early 1980s, the accounts payable department of a US car company. 500 people work there. A Japanese company runs the same department with about 100. Five times fewer. The US company wants to close that gap. Before you see what they found, make the first call yourself.
segments.build: 500 vs ~100 counters, 5x; STOP 1 at segment end

segments.narration: Mapping revealed the real reason. Most of the work went into manually reconciling three separate documents. The gap was not closed by faster systems for the existing process. Instead, the process itself was rewritten: payment is now triggered directly from the receipt record, with no separate invoice. Per reports, the headcount needed fell by about 75 percent.
segments.build: Three documents; bolt bounces off; receipt record arrow to payment; ~75% counter with per reports

segments.narration: Case two. A Swedish fintech, per public reports, 2024 to 2025. An AI agent starts handling its customer conversations: about 2.3 million a month. Per reports, the drop in service load is on the scale of about 700 service reps. Handling time falls from about 11 minutes to under two.
segments.build: Counters build one by one, per reports chip stays

segments.narration: These figures come from company publications and media reports. They're here for learning, not as proof that people should be replaced. Then, by early 2025, the company starts rehiring human service reps. On simple requests, the AI performed about as well as people. On complex ones, like disputes or personally difficult cases, quality dropped noticeably. So what went wrong? Decide before you hear it.
onScreen: for learning, not proof people should be replaced
segments.build: Disclaimer line; rehiring; split simple / complex; STOP 2 at segment end

segments.narration: Management admitted that focusing too much on efficiency hurt service quality. The fix was a hybrid model: AI for the routine, a person when empathy and judgment are needed.
segments.build: Split: AI chip 'routine' / person icon 'empathy + judgment'; 'hybrid model'

segments.narration: Two cases, decades apart, with completely different technology. The same lesson. Process mapping is not a bureaucratic step. It's what separates a change that works from a change that has to be fixed after the fact. And notice: both stories are told in numbers. Headcount, handling time, quality. Without a number, nobody can check a change.
segments.build: Both cases side by side; 'map first'; three numbers; next-step chip

segments.narration: This is the HR case from Lesson 1: a services company with about 400 employees. HR gets about 90 requests a month, most of them repeats: vacation days, pension, expenses, overtime. They arrive by WhatsApp, by email, and in person, with no system. Nobody knows how many need human judgment.
The tempting first move is a chatbot. Not yet. First we map, AS-IS: how it actually happens on a normal day. No fixing, no AI.

Field 1 is the process name, plain and specific: answering employees' repeat questions to HR. Field 2 is the trigger, the concrete thing that starts the process: a message, a form, a date. Before I fill it in, you choose.
All three channels go on the map, because all three really happen. Where a process starts and ends is a decision. Without clear boundaries, it swells until it covers the whole organization.

Field 3 is the steps, each with a role owner. Here there are three: receiving the request, checking the topic, then an answer or an escalation. Owners are roles, not names, so the map stays true when people change.
Each role gets its own lane, so you can always see who is holding the work. Field 4 asks where responsibility passes from one role to another.

From HR staff to the HR manager, when a question goes beyond known policy. That's the most dangerous moment in a process: the staffer assumes the manager knows what happened before. A good map marks each handoff: from whom, to whom, what passes, and what if the receiver is unavailable. Here, there's no single channel for it.

Field 5 is knowledge sources: the vacation, pension, expense, and overtime policies. Each gets an owner, here the HR manager, and a sensitivity tag: public, internal, confidential, or restricted. These policies are internal. An employee's personal or financial details are confidential, and never go into a public AI tool.
Field 6 is existing controls. Is anything checking the answers before they go out? What goes in the map?
No formal control: it depends on the staffer's own judgment. That's a valid answer, and exactly what mapping reveals.
Field 7 is gaps, and here you can write unclear. Nobody knows how many wrong answers were given, and there's no single handoff channel. That's a diagnostic result.

Field 8 is the success metric. Today, about 35 percent of the HR team's time goes to repeat questions. Target: 20 percent within three months. A number you can check later. Next, you fill Field 5 yourself.

screens.hint: Open any field to read it. Then select two and press Check.
screens.question: Which two fields together show the risk at the HR handoff?

tiles.title: Name
tiles.text: Answering employees' repeat questions to HR
tiles.feedback: This field does not follow the question once it leaves the first staffer.

tiles.title: Trigger
tiles.text: A question by WhatsApp, email, or in person
tiles.feedback: This field does not follow the question once it leaves the first staffer.

tiles.title: Steps
tiles.text: Receiving the request (employee) to checking the topic (HR staff) to answer or escalation (HR staff / manager)
tiles.feedback: Field 3 shows who does each step, not the moment between them or what can go wrong there.

tiles.title: Handoffs
tiles.text: From HR staff to HR manager when policy is exceeded
tiles.feedback: Field 4 shows the question moving from HR staff to the HR manager.

tiles.title: Sources
tiles.text: Vacation, pension, expense, overtime policy. Owner: HR manager. Tag: INTERNAL
tiles.feedback: This field does not follow the question once it leaves the first staffer.

tiles.title: Controls
tiles.text: No formal control: depends on the staffer's personal judgment
tiles.feedback: Field 6 is about how answers get checked. It says nothing about the handoff.

tiles.title: Gaps
tiles.text: Unclear how many wrong answers were given; no single handoff channel
tiles.feedback: Field 7 adds the risk: no single channel for that handoff.

tiles.title: Metric
tiles.text: Baseline ~35% of HR time on repeat questions. Target 20% within 3 months
tiles.feedback: This field does not follow the question once it leaves the first staffer.

screens.instruction: Answer one question, or skip the challenge.
screens.hint: Answer if you can already judge where AI fits. Skipping costs nothing.

image.alt: A staff member reading through a case file at a desk

top.text: Optional challenge. Right on the first try? Skip to this chapter's last task.

middle.text: Which decision needs clear human judgment, not AI?

options.label: Deciding whether a customer is eligible
options.feedback: Right on the first try: you can jump to the last task of this chapter, or take the full chapter.

options.label: Summarizing a long request in three lines
options.feedback: Free text into a short summary is a good fit, with a person checking. The full chapter starts now.

options.label: Tagging a request by its topic
options.feedback: Tagging is a low-risk classification, a good fit. Look for rights or money at stake. The full chapter starts now.

screens.instruction: Set where the HR process starts and ends.
screens.hint: Look for what starts it from outside, and who picks up the result.

options.feedback: WhatsApp and in-person questions never reach the inbox, and nobody receives anything at the end. Most of the process sits outside.

options.end: the question reaches the HR manager.
options.feedback: Escalation passes the work on. The employee is still waiting, so the process has not delivered its output yet.
The map opens at the external trigger and closes when the employee gets an answer, even after an escalation.

screens.instruction: Choose what the map must record at this handoff.
screens.hint: Think about the moment responsibility changes hands.

image.alt: An empty desk at the end of the day, a stack of papers waiting on it

top.text: A question exceeds policy. It goes to the HR manager, who is away.

options.label: A rule naming a backup manager
options.feedback: Your AS-IS map now shows a rule nobody follows today. The real gap disappears before anyone has measured it.

options.label: From whom, to whom, what passes, if unavailable
options.feedback: Field 4 now shows sender, receiver, what passes, and the unavailable case. Here nothing covers it, so Field 7 records it.

options.label: Nothing: the manager knows the history
options.feedback: The map now assumes the receiver knows what happened before. When the manager is away, the question has no path.

options.label: An AI agent to reroute questions
options.feedback: The map now describes a tool that does not exist. Lesson 5 would start from a plan, not from today.

screens.instruction: Choose the first question to ask about this bottleneck.
screens.hint: A bottleneck is a step limited by the slowest resource. Before speed, ask why.

image.alt: A coordinator reading a tall stack of printed course feedback by hand

top.text: One step: the coordinator prints and reads all feedback by hand, 3 to 4 hours per course.

options.label: Why did this step form, and is it needed?
options.feedback: The cause decides the fix. Sometimes the right fix is to remove the step, not speed it up, as in the car-company case.

options.label: Which AI tool summarizes feedback fastest?
options.feedback: You would speed up a step without knowing why it formed. Faster technology on an unmapped process locks the problem in.

options.label: How many more coordinators can we hire?
options.feedback: More people on the same step keep it in place. First ask whether the step should exist.

screens.instruction: Sort each card: which good-fit kind, or poor fit?
screens.hint: Select a card, then a column.

feedback.correct: Good fit, unstructured to structured: free text in, a structured topic out.
feedback.wrong: Look at what goes in and what comes out. Is a judgment call at stake here?

feedback.correct: Poor fit: irreversible, money at stake. Per reports, the fintech's quality dropped on complex cases and it moved to a hybrid model.
feedback.wrong: If this decision is wrong, who carries the loss, and can it be undone?

feedback.correct: Good fit, low-risk decision point: it can be accelerated, with a person watching where risk rises.
feedback.wrong: Ask how much damage one wrong label would cause, and how fast it would be caught.

cards.text: Fix disorder in how requests arrive

feedback.correct: Poor fit, a process problem: nothing is missing but order. AI on top keeps the disorder running faster.
feedback.wrong: Is information missing here, or is the process itself disorganized?

feedback.correct: Poor fit: you cannot build on unknown foundations. This needs diagnosis, not more technology.
feedback.wrong: Check what the map actually knows before anything is built on it.

feedback.correct: Good fit, handoff with delay or loss: AI documents it, so the HR manager gets the history.
feedback.wrong: Think about what the HR manager receives today when a question is passed on.

screens.instruction: Sort each case into the mistake it shows.
screens.hint: Read the case, then choose the bin that names its mistake.

cards.text: Fields 6 and 7 were left blank to finish the map quickly.

feedback.correct: Controls and gaps are where the findings live. Skipping them leaves Lesson 5 nothing to protect against.
feedback.wrong: The map has a goal and matches today. Look at which fields were never filled.

cards.text: The map shows how HR intends requests to flow, not how they flow today.

feedback.correct: The map now describes a wish. Every gap on a normal day stays hidden.
feedback.wrong: Nothing was skipped or automated. Compare the map with a normal day in HR.

cards.text: A chatbot is planned for the three channels exactly as they run today.

feedback.correct: The most critical mistake. Three channels with no organized system get faster, and the disorder grows with them.
feedback.wrong: The map may be accurate. Look at what is about to be done with the process.

cards.text: HR moved to one request form. The map still shows three channels.

feedback.correct: The map was right once. Lesson 5 would now build on a process that no longer exists.
feedback.wrong: Something changed after the map was drawn. Which mistake follows a change?

cards.text: Someone mapped every HR task 'to have it documented', with no question to answer.

feedback.correct: Without a question, nobody can say which process or boundaries matter. The map grows and decides nothing.
feedback.wrong: The map may be accurate and complete. Ask what it was drawn to decide.

sources: Cases constructed (FL12); D is a fictional later change

screens.instruction: Map three fields of a case that is not HR.
screens.hint: Same eight fields, different case. Select a card, then a column.

feedback.correct: Placed. A concrete event starts the work, as in HR, but here it repeats 8 to 12 times a day per rep.
feedback.wrong: Ask what has to happen before any summary can be written.

cards.text: The rep updates the CRM, often late

feedback.correct: Placed. The step and its owner, written as it really runs: often late, not as the rule says.
feedback.wrong: This is work a role does. Where do steps and owners go?

cards.text: Unclear whether reps see a problem

feedback.correct: Placed. An honest unknown. It tells you what to ask before Lesson 5.
feedback.wrong: Nobody knows this yet. Which field holds what is missing or unclear?

cards.text: An AI tool drafts each call summary

feedback.correct: Kept out. Your Homework 2 AI step is a future idea too. It stays off your AS-IS map.
feedback.wrong: Does this happen on a normal day today, or is it an idea for later?

screens.hint: Before you write anything, remove names and identifying details.

image.alt: Someone writing up notes on a laptop and in a notebook

top.text: The workbook has a live AI coach that reads what you type.

options.label: Your real map, with names and policy titles
options.feedback: Names and internal policy now sit in an AI tool. Personal, employee or financial details are CONFIDENTIAL: keep them out.

options.label: Roles instead of names, no identifying details
options.feedback: Nothing identifying leaves your hands. If unsure whether something is allowed, the Lesson 3 rule applies: leave it out.

options.label: Your real map, with Field 5 left empty
options.feedback: Names can sit in any field, not only Field 5. Steps and handoffs still identify people.

privacy.text: Leave out names and identifying details.

screens.instruction: Check your map against three questions. Then pick your biggest risk.
screens.hint: Answer honestly. 'Not yet' sends you back with one fix.

rows.text: Does every step name who exactly does it?

feedback.yes: Every step has an owner. Lesson 5 can place AI or a person next to each one.
feedback.notYet: A step without a role cannot be improved or monitored. Name the role, or write 'unclear' in Field 7.

rows.text: Does Field 4 say what happens if the receiver is unavailable?

feedback.yes: Your handoffs cover the unavailable case. Delays now show up on the map, not in daily work.
feedback.notYet: A handoff with no plan stalls. Add what happens, or record it as a gap.

rows.text: Can a number show that the metric improved?

feedback.yes: You can check your change later: baseline now, target to check against.
feedback.notYet: Without a number, nobody can tell whether anything improved. Add a baseline, even estimated, and a target.

chips.label: Ideal, not actual
chips.feedback: Reread Field 3 against a normal day, not the written procedure.

chips.label: No clear goal
chips.feedback: Write one sentence on what this map must help decide.

chips.label: Rushed mapping
chips.feedback: Reopen Fields 6 and 7. Those are the ones skipped first.

chips.label: Not updated
chips.feedback: Note the date on your map and what would trigger an update.

chips.label: Automating a broken process
chips.feedback: Before Lesson 5, list which steps need fixing, not speeding up.

steps.strip: Before Lesson 5: every field filled, metric measurable, no invented answers.

screens.instruction: Choose one. Your first answer counts.
screens.hint: Choose one. You can retry, but only the first answer counts.

items.stem: Lesson 1 case: customer service. Field 4 says 'Rep to department.' What is missing?

options.label: A rule that reps must route correctly
options.feedback: That adds a rule nobody follows today. The map becomes a redesign before the gaps are known.

options.label: The AI tool that will route requests
options.feedback: The map now holds a future tool, and today's handoff stays as vague as before.

options.label: What passes, and what if nobody is available
options.feedback: From and to are there. Without what passes and the unavailable case, a request stalls between teams.

options.label: Nothing more: the department sees the request
options.feedback: The receiver may not know what happened before. The map hides the most dangerous moment in the process.

items.stem: Lesson 1 case: student inquiries. Which step suits AI first?

options.label: Deciding on exceptional student requests
options.feedback: Exceptional requests need human judgment. An error here can touch a student's rights.

options.label: Tagging each inquiry by topic for routing
options.feedback: Unstructured text in, a structured label out, at low risk. Exceptions still go to a person.

options.label: Handling sensitive cases on its own
options.feedback: Sensitive cases need judgment, and today nobody knows how they are handled. That is unclear, not ready.

options.label: Answering by category before categories are counted
options.feedback: There is no breakdown of categories yet. A solution here stands on unknown foundations.

items.stem: Lesson 1 case: weekly report, 4 to 6 hours. Nothing is logged. Baseline?

options.label: About 5 hours, marked as estimated
options.feedback: An estimated metric beats no metric. You now have a starting number to check the target against.

options.label: Nothing until a time log exists
options.feedback: Field 8 stays empty. In three months, nobody can show whether anything changed.

options.label: The target time, once it is set
options.feedback: Field 8 now shows where the team hopes to land and nothing about where it stands now.

options.label: 'Much faster reports' for now
options.feedback: That is a feeling, not a number. Nobody could check it later.

items.stem: Lesson 1 case: customer service. Share of simple requests unknown. Where does this go?

options.label: Field 6: reps double-check each request
options.feedback: That records a control nobody reported. Lesson 5 would rely on a check that may not exist.

options.label: Field 3: add a sorting step
options.feedback: That adds a step while mapping. The unknown share stays off the map.

options.label: Field 8: target fewer complex requests
options.feedback: A target with no baseline, while the real problem, that nobody knows the share, stays hidden.

options.label: Field 7: 'unclear', to investigate first
options.feedback: A diagnostic result, not a weakness. It shows what to check before Lesson 5 and what not to build on yet.

options.label: Mapping is a condition, not bureaucracy
options.feedback: Process mapping is a condition for change that lasts. Your map is now the raw material for Lesson 5.

options.label: 'Unclear' is a legitimate answer
options.feedback: Not a failure of the mapper, a diagnostic result. Your Field 7 lists what to investigate first.

options.label: Not every bottleneck needs acceleration
options.feedback: Sometimes the right fix is to remove the step, not speed it up. Ask why it formed first.
